title: Large or Small Values for K (CyberLearn)

children.text: Many reversible reactions have very large or very small values for their equilibrium constant,

. That is, one reaction (either the forward or the reverse) is much stronger than the other reaction. For instance, most acid-base reactions, precipitation reactions and redox reactions have either a very large or a very small
For reactions with intermediate values of
, determining the concentrations of the chemical species at equilibrium often leads to complex algebraic manipulations. However, when
is very large or very small, we can use a much simpler, two-step approach described here.

The two step approach simplifies the algebra and allows us to reason qualitatively about chemical reactions and their effects on the chemical concentrations. This qualitative reasoning is essential to understanding many applications of chemical equilibrium. We will first discuss the strategy of this two-step process and then demonstrate worked examples.
Step 1: Determine the concentrations of the majority species assuming the reaction goes to completion.
We need to determine which chemical species will have large concentrations at equilibrium. If

is very large, we can assume the reaction will progress nearly all the way to the right (mostly products). We can think of this as a forward reaction progressing to completion and assume for practical purposes that
is very small, we can assume the reaction will lie nearly all the way to the left (mostly reactants). We can make the approximation that
is not just small by infinitely small, i.e.
= 0. We can think of this as a reverse reaction progressing to completion.
These assumptions lead to a limiting reagent calculation. For
= infinity, the forward reaction goes all the way to completion, i.e. until one of the reactants runs out. For

= 0, the reverse reaction proceeds to completion (towards reactants) until one of the products runs out. In either case, the reaction progresses until one or more of the chemical species runs out. Under this assumption, at completion some of the chemical species have non-zero concentrations and one or more (the limiting reagent(s)) have zero concentration.

is either 0 or infinity. Under these assumptions, some chemical species (the limiting reagent(s)) are completely consumed and so have zero concentration. However, in equilibrium systems both forward and reverse reactions are constantly occurring, so we know that no species will have a zero concnentration. Instead, the concentrations of the "limiting reagents" are present in very small amounts, and we call these the minority species.
Step 2: Determine the concentration of the minority specie(s) using the determined equilibrium concentrations for all other species and the equilibrium expression.

is very large or very small, we can assume that the equilibrium concentrations of the majority species are very close to the values we found in step 1. In Step 2, we determine the concentrations of the minority species at equilibrium using the determined equilibrium concentrations for all other species and the equilibrium expression.
This two-step procedure allows us to approximate equilibrium values when the equilibrium constant,

, is either very large or small. To make sure our assumptions hold for a given situation, we compare the concentrations of the minority species to that of the majority species. If our assumption is valid, the concentrations of the minority species will be much smaller than that of the majority species (e.g., less than 5% of the majority.)
